title: Nobody tricked a customer. The bank paid itself out.
technique: Supplier breach, fake IBANs and instant transfers
audience: Bank security, payments and fraud teams, companies that give suppliers access to their systems, and anyone who reads 'AI heist' headlines
subject: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa cyberattack, November 2026
summary: According to its chair, attackers who entered Crédit Mutuel Arkéa through a compromised supplier created fake IBANs at its online bank Fortuneo and sent about €100 million from the bank's own account by instant transfer to accounts at other European banks, then into crypto. He says the attack was very probably assisted by advanced AI; no evidence of that has been published.
lesson: A supplier breach is your breach until proven otherwise: cut and review every access the supplier had, not just the link you saw. Instant transfers settle before anyone looks, so new beneficiaries and unusual outflows from an institution's own accounts need limits and a human check. And 'AI-enabled' in a headline is a claim, not a finding: the documented mechanism here is old-fashioned access, fake accounts and mule accounts opened in advance.
claim: A heist 'of a new kind', run by AI
counterclaim: Supplier access, fake IBANs, instant transfers
observations: On 27 October the bank detected signs that a supplier's information system was compromised and cut the link between the two systems; at that point, the chair says, nothing suggested the attackers could reach the bank.

From Sunday 1 November, the attackers generated fake IBANs in the name of Fortuneo, the group's online bank, to trigger payment orders from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account, not from client accounts.
They chose instant transfers which, the chair notes, by nature carry fewer checks than ordinary transfers, and a weekend start.

The money went first to real accounts opened in advance at other European banks, then to crypto platforms to blur the trail; the chair reads the advance account opening as a sign the attack was long prepared.

Crypto specialists noticed abnormal transactions on the Sunday and Monday, and the investigator ZachXBT made the fraud public, but the bank only measured the scale on the Tuesday morning and then cut all external access.
source_summary: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa announced on 4 November 2026 that a 'sophisticated attack coming from the outside' had caused fraudulent transfers of around €100 million from its own account to other banks, that the attack was contained and that clients suffered no losses (AFP). The Paris prosecutor opened an investigation into an attack on an automated data processing system by an organised group. Le Télégramme reported a higher figure (133 million), which the bank did not confirm. In an AFP interview on 13 November, reported by Silicon.fr and INCYBER, chair Julien Carmona described the timeline: supplier compromise detected on 27 October; fake Fortuneo IBANs used from 1 November to trigger payment orders from the bank's own account; instant transfers to real accounts at other European banks, then crypto platforms; discovery of the scale on 3 November. He put the loss at about €100 million, around 1% of the group's equity, said part of the money had been recovered or frozen, called the attack unprecedented in sophistication and 'very probably' assisted by advanced artificial intelligence, and said the perpetrators are unknown.
limits: This case rests on the bank's own statements and press reporting; no court has ruled and the perpetrators are unidentified. The role of artificial intelligence is the chair's assessment ('very probably'), and none of the sources publishes evidence of what, if anything, AI did; the headline figure of $110 million is a currency conversion of about €100 million, and the gross amount diverted may be higher. It is not public how the supplier was breached or how the fake IBANs were accepted. Nothing here suggests that Fortuneo or Crédit Mutuel Arkéa customers lost money; they were not the targets.
assessment: Documented fraud · victim's own statements and press reporting
assessment_source: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa via AFP; Silicon.fr; INCYBER

es.short_title: El atraco de 100 millones con IBAN falsos
es.technique: Proveedor comprometido, IBAN falsos y transferencias inmediatas
es.subject: Ciberataque contra Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, noviembre de 2026
es.summary: Según su presidente, unos atacantes que entraron en Crédit Mutuel Arkéa a través de un proveedor comprometido crearon IBAN falsos de su banco online Fortuneo y sacaron unos 100 millones de euros de la cuenta propia del banco con transferencias inmediatas a cuentas en otros bancos europeos, y de ahí a criptomonedas. Dice que el ataque estuvo muy probablemente ayudado por IA avanzada; no se ha publicado ninguna prueba de ello.
es.lesson: La brecha de un proveedor es tu brecha mientras no se demuestre lo contrario: corta y revisa todos los accesos que tenía, no solo el enlace que has visto. Las transferencias inmediatas se liquidan antes de que nadie mire, así que los beneficiarios nuevos y las salidas inusuales de las cuentas propias de una entidad necesitan límites y una comprobación humana. Y «con IA» en un titular es una afirmación, no un hallazgo: el mecanismo documentado aquí es de toda la vida — accesos, cuentas falsas y cuentas mula abiertas de antemano.
es.claim: Un atraco «de nuevo tipo», hecho por IA
es.counterclaim: Acceso de proveedor, IBAN falsos, transferencias inmediatas
es.audience: Equipos de seguridad, pagos y fraude de bancos, empresas que dan acceso a sus sistemas a proveedores, y cualquiera que lea titulares de «atraco con IA»
observations: El 27 de octubre el banco detectó indicios de que el sistema de información de un proveedor estaba comprometido y cortó la conexión entre ambos; en ese momento, dice el presidente, nada hacía pensar que los atacantes pudieran llegar al banco.

Desde el domingo 1 de noviembre, los atacantes generaron IBAN falsos a nombre de Fortuneo, el banco online del grupo, para lanzar órdenes de pago desde la cuenta propia de Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, no desde cuentas de clientes.
Eligieron transferencias inmediatas, que según el presidente llevan por naturaleza menos controles que las ordinarias, y empezaron en fin de semana.

El dinero fue primero a cuentas reales abiertas de antemano en otros bancos europeos y después a plataformas de criptomonedas para borrar el rastro; el presidente ve en esas cuentas previas la señal de un ataque preparado con mucho tiempo.

Especialistas en cripto vieron transacciones anómalas el domingo y el lunes, y el investigador ZachXBT hizo público el fraude, pero el banco no midió el alcance hasta la mañana del martes, cuando cortó todos los accesos externos.
es.source_summary: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa anunció el 4 de noviembre de 2026 que un «ataque sofisticado procedente del exterior» había provocado transferencias fraudulentas de unos 100 millones de euros desde su cuenta propia hacia otros bancos, que el ataque estaba contenido y que los clientes no sufrieron pérdidas (AFP). La fiscalía de París abrió una investigación por ataque a un sistema de tratamiento automatizado de datos por banda organizada. Le Télégramme publicó una cifra mayor (133 millones), que el banco no confirmó. En una entrevista con AFP el 13 de noviembre, recogida por Silicon.fr e INCYBER, el presidente Julien Carmona describió la cronología: compromiso del proveedor detectado el 27 de octubre; IBAN falsos de Fortuneo usados desde el 1 de noviembre para lanzar órdenes de pago desde la cuenta propia del banco; transferencias inmediatas a cuentas reales en otros bancos europeos y después a plataformas cripto; descubrimiento del alcance el 3 de noviembre. Cifró la pérdida en unos 100 millones de euros, en torno al 1 % de los fondos propios del grupo, dijo que parte del dinero se ha recuperado o congelado, calificó el ataque de inédito en sofisticación y «muy probablemente» ayudado por inteligencia artificial avanzada, y dijo que se desconoce a los autores.
es.limits: Este caso se apoya en las declaraciones del propio banco y en la prensa; ningún tribunal se ha pronunciado y los autores no están identificados. El papel de la inteligencia artificial es una valoración del presidente («muy probablemente»), y ninguna fuente publica pruebas de qué hizo la IA, si es que hizo algo; los 110 millones de dólares del titular son la conversión de unos 100 millones de euros, y el importe bruto desviado podría ser mayor. No se ha hecho público cómo se comprometió al proveedor ni cómo se aceptaron los IBAN falsos. Nada de lo que aquí se dice indica que clientes de Fortuneo o de Crédit Mutuel Arkéa perdieran dinero; no eran el objetivo.
es.assessment: Fraude documentado · declaraciones de la víctima y prensa
es.assessment_source: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa vía AFP; Silicon.fr; INCYBER

title: A message from the CEO. A call from the lawyer. Neither was real.
technique: Executive impersonation with an AI-cloned voice
audience: Executives, treasury and finance teams, and anyone who can authorise a payment on someone else's instruction
subject: Fideuram (Intesa Sanpaolo group) transfer fraud, February 2026
summary: According to Reuters, fraudsters posing as Intesa Sanpaolo's chief executive on WhatsApp, then as a law-firm partner on a call with an AI-cloned voice, got the chairman of its private-banking arm Fideuram to order about €95 million in transfers abroad. About €36 million is still missing.
lesson: Seniority and a familiar voice are not authorisation. An urgent, confidential transfer request must be confirmed by calling the person back on a number you already hold, and pass the normal dual-approval process, however senior the requester and however convincing the second voice that 'confirms' it.
counterclaim: Call back on a number you already hold
observations: The first contact came through WhatsApp, a channel outside the bank's own systems, from someone presenting as the group's chief executive.
The request carried the classic pressure of CEO fraud: urgent help with an overseas transaction.
A second, apparently independent party then 'confirmed' the instruction by phone: a caller presenting as a senior partner at a prominent law firm, whose voice Reuters says was replicated with AI.
The victim was himself a senior executive, and the order went through his own finance department: authority inside the organisation carried the fraud past the usual checks.
The money went mainly to accounts in China and Hong Kong and, according to Reuters, part of it was converted into cryptocurrency.
source_summary: Reuters reported on 25 September 2026, citing sources, that the fraud began in February 2026, when the then-chairman of Fideuram received a WhatsApp message that appeared to come from Intesa Sanpaolo's CEO asking for urgent help with an overseas transaction, followed by a call from someone posing as a senior partner at a prominent law firm, whose voice was replicated with AI. He instructed the finance department to make a series of transfers, mainly to China and Hong Kong, totalling about €95 million. About €53 million was recovered through cooperation between authorities in China, Portugal and Italy; about €36 million has not been traced after passing through overseas accounts and being converted into cryptocurrency. Milan prosecutors have placed a foreign national living outside Europe under investigation for computer fraud; no Fideuram executive is under investigation. The chairman resigned in March 2026 citing personal reasons. Intesa Sanpaolo and Fideuram declined to comment. Il Sole 24 Ore separately reports the same amounts (€40 million recovered from a Chinese bank and €13 million from a Portuguese one) and the use of AI to replicate the lawyer's voice.
limits: This case rests on press reports based on unnamed sources; Intesa Sanpaolo and Fideuram declined to comment, and no court has ruled. The AI voice cloning is as described by the reporting, not verified here, and neither source publishes the messages or the recording. It is not established how the voice sample was obtained or whether other institutions were targeted. Nothing here suggests that the executives impersonated were involved; they were the identities the fraudsters borrowed.
assessment: Documented fraud · press reporting from unnamed sources

title: It knows the train you took. That is what makes it dangerous.
short_title: The phishing that knows your trip
subject: Renfe and Adif data breach, 2026
summary: A leak that links passengers to real journeys could let fraudsters write refund or booking messages that mention trips you actually made. No such attack has been reported yet.
lesson: A message that knows real details of your life is not proof that it is genuine. Leaked data can supply those details. Check any refund or booking incident by opening the operator's app or website yourself, never through the link or number in the message.
message: Hello [your name], we are contacting you about your journey Madrid – Valencia on 14 September, seat 7C. Due to the service incident on that route you are entitled to a €38.40 refund. To receive it, confirm your details and your card within 24 hours: [link]
counterclaim: Real trip details, from leaked data
observations: The attacker opens with facts the victim recognises: their name, a real route and date, perhaps a seat.
The pretext fits the travel: a refund for a disrupted journey, or an incident with a booking.
Familiar details lower suspicion, so the request for card or identity data at the end feels routine.
Unlike generic phishing, each message can be different and personal, which makes it harder to recognise as a campaign.
source_summary: Xataka, drawing on an El Mundo analysis confirmed by Adif, reports that a cyberattack on Adif reached interconnected Renfe systems and exposed about 500 GB and over 150 million records: identity data (names, national ID numbers, phone numbers, emails, dates of birth, postal addresses) and about 100 million nominative ticket records that can be cross-referenced to reconstruct passengers' travel. The article itself warns that an attacker could use this to write credible messages about a supposed ticket refund or a booking incident. It states that bank and payment data were not compromised.
limits: This is an anticipated scenario, not a documented case: there is no known case of this fraud yet. The message is invented by the observatory for illustration; its route, date, seat and amount are fictional, and it does not reproduce any real message or any real person's data. The breach figures are those reported by the cited source and are not independently verified here. Nothing here suggests that Renfe or Adif send such messages.
assessment: Emerging threat · possible, not yet observed
assessment_source: Digital Fraud Observatory, from Xataka reporting

es.title: Sabe qué tren cogiste. Eso es lo que lo hace peligroso.
es.short_title: El phishing que conoce tu viaje
es.subject: Filtración de datos de Renfe y Adif, 2026
es.summary: Una filtración que vincula a los pasajeros con viajes reales permitiría a los estafadores escribir mensajes sobre devoluciones o reservas que mencionan trayectos que de verdad hiciste. De momento no hay constancia de ningún ataque así.
es.lesson: Que un mensaje conozca detalles reales de tu vida no demuestra que sea auténtico: los datos filtrados pueden aportar esos detalles. Comprueba cualquier devolución o incidencia con una reserva entrando tú mismo en la app o la web del operador, nunca a través del enlace o el teléfono del mensaje.
es.message: Hola [tu nombre], te escribimos por tu viaje Madrid – Valencia del 14 de septiembre, plaza 7C. Por la incidencia en el servicio de esa ruta tienes derecho a un reembolso de 38,40 €. Para recibirlo, confirma tus datos y tu tarjeta en las próximas 24 horas: [enlace]
es.claim: Tu viaje del 14 de septiembre: reembolso de 38,40 €
es.counterclaim: Datos reales del viaje, sacados de una filtración
observations: El atacante empieza con datos que la víctima reconoce: su nombre, una ruta y una fecha reales, quizá hasta la plaza.
El pretexto encaja con el viaje: el reembolso de un trayecto con incidencias, o un problema con una reserva.
Los detalles conocidos bajan la guardia, y la petición final de la tarjeta o de datos personales parece un trámite.
A diferencia del phishing genérico, cada mensaje puede ser distinto y personal, lo que hace más difícil reconocerlo como una campaña.
es.source_summary: Xataka, a partir de un análisis de El Mundo confirmado por Adif, informa de que un ciberataque contra Adif alcanzó sistemas interconectados de Renfe y expuso unos 500 GB y más de 150 millones de registros: datos de identidad (nombres, DNI, teléfonos, correos electrónicos, fechas de nacimiento, direcciones postales) y unos 100 millones de registros de billetes nominativos que pueden cruzarse para reconstruir los viajes de los pasajeros. El propio artículo advierte de que un atacante podría usarlo para escribir mensajes creíbles sobre una supuesta devolución de un billete o una incidencia con una reserva. Según el artículo, los datos bancarios y de pago no se vieron comprometidos.
es.limits: Es un escenario anticipado, no un caso documentado: todavía no hay constancia de este fraude. El mensaje lo ha escrito el observatorio como ilustración; la ruta, la fecha, la plaza y el importe son ficticios, y no reproduce ningún mensaje real ni datos de ninguna persona real. Las cifras de la filtración son las que publica la fuente citada y no se han verificado de forma independiente aquí. Nada de lo que aquí se dice indica que Renfe o Adif envíen mensajes así.
es.assessment: Amenaza emergente · posible, aún no observada
es.assessment_source: Digital Fraud Observatory, a partir de lo publicado por Xataka

title: A lawful-looking request. A disclosure to the wrong party.
audience: Banks, fintechs, legal and compliance teams; affected customers as data subjects
subject: Revolut customer-data disclosure after fraudulent government-domain requests
summary: Revolut confirmed that sensitive customer data was disclosed after fraudulent information requests were sent from a legitimate government-agency email domain.
lesson: For regulated firms, a trusted domain is not enough. Sensitive data requests need independent requester verification, authority checks and escalation paths before records leave the institution.
counterclaim: Requester authority must be independently verified
observations: The reported attack targeted a compliance workflow rather than a public scam landing page.

title: A dead website's name. Someone else's business behind it.
audience: Bloggers, librarians, Wikipedia editors and anyone who maintains old web pages with links
subject: en-html.org
summary: Emails written as if from the owners of defunct websites ask site administrators to swap old links for "mirror" copies on en-html.org. The copies are named after closed charities, archives and local history projects, and now redirect to commercial hotel sites.
lesson: A request to update an old link is not proof that it comes from the original owner. Check the new address before changing anything. If the original site is gone, link to an archive.org copy instead of a "mirror" offered by a stranger.
claim: We are the owners of the site you link to
counterclaim: Why does the new link end on a hotel website?
observations: On 9 October 2026 a site administrator reported receiving emails from people posing as the legitimate owners of expired domains he had linked to, asking him to point those links to copies hosted on en-html.org.

On 14 October 2026 the en-html.org home page showed "Under Maintenance" and linked to 23 subdomains named after defunct organisations, such as sharksavers, minneapolishistorical, ancient-egypt and fairmountpark.

On the same day sharksavers.en-html.org answered with a permanent redirect (HTTP 301) to a page on beachhotel.net titled "Shark Savers: Protecting the Oceans, One Shark at a Time | Beachhotel.net", and minneapolishistorical.en-html.org redirected to a page on hotelsdowntown.info.
en-html.org was registered on 28 April 2025 through Spaceship, Inc.
source_summary: Russell Coker documented the emails and the en-html.org mirrors on his blog on 9 October 2026 and recommends replacing such links with archive.org copies. The redirects to hotel websites were observed by the Digital Fraud Observatory on 14 October 2026.
limits: The aim of building search ranking from old links is the source's inference; it is not confirmed by the operator. This case does not show that anyone lost money or that the hotel sites commissioned the scheme. The redirects can change at any time; they are described as they stood on 14 October 2026.
